unitLessons.title: Quadratic relations and three useful forms
unitLessons.outcome: Understand that standard, factored, and vertex forms expose different features of one function.

opening.prompt: Compare three formulas for the same trajectory.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make quadratic relations and three useful forms necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for quadratic relations and three useful forms.
exposition: Understand that standard, factored, and vertex forms expose different features of one function. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In quadratic relations and three useful forms, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Same parabola with three formulas. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Feature table. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.title: Graphing parabolas

opening.prompt: Sketch a parabola from a few structural features.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make graphing parabolas necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for graphing parabolas.
exposition: Use opening, scale, symmetry, vertex, and intercepts to construct a graph. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In graphing parabolas, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Parameter sliders. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Symmetry fold. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.outcome: Factor, expand, or complete the square according to the question being asked.

opening.prompt: Reveal zeros, intercept, or optimum from the same function.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make moving among forms necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for moving among forms.
exposition: Factor, expand, or complete the square according to the question being asked. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In moving among forms, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Strategic conversion triangle. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Preserved features. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

opening.prompt: Sketch a parabola from a few structural features.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make graphing parabolas necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.

exposition: Use opening, scale, symmetry, vertex, and intercepts to construct a graph. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In graphing parabolas, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Parameter sliders. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Symmetry fold. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Vertex form and transformations
lesson.outcome: Read shifts, scale, and extrema from a(x-h)^2+k.

opening.prompt: Move and stretch a parent parabola.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make vertex form and transformations necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.

exposition: Read shifts, scale, and extrema from a(x-h)^2+k. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In vertex form and transformations, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Parent transformation. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Coordinate mapping. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Combine zeros, sign intervals, and graph position to find solution regions. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In quadratic inequalities, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Parabola above/below regions. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Sign chart. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.title: Rational expressions and restrictions
unitLessons.outcome: Determine where a denominator is zero and state the valid input set.

opening.prompt: Identify forbidden settings in a rate or formula.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make rational expressions and restrictions necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for rational expressions and restrictions.
exposition: Determine where a denominator is zero and state the valid input set. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In rational expressions and restrictions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Denominator-zero detector. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Domain number line. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

opening.prompt: Combine two rational scaling relationships.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make multiplication of rational expressions necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.

exposition: Factor before multiplying and cancel across products. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In multiplication of rational expressions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Factor grid. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Before-after cancellation. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.title: Addition and subtraction
unitLessons.outcome: Create equivalent rational expressions with a common denominator before combining numerators.

opening.prompt: Combine two fractional rates or parts.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make addition and subtraction necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for addition and subtraction.
exposition: Create equivalent rational expressions with a common denominator before combining numerators. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In addition and subtraction, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Shared-denominator construction. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Sign-distribution panel. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

opening.prompt: Identify forbidden settings in a rate or formula.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make rational expressions and restrictions necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for rational expressions and restrictions.
exposition: Determine where a denominator is zero and state the valid input set. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In rational expressions and restrictions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Denominator-zero detector. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Domain number line. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Addition and subtraction
lesson.outcome: Create equivalent rational expressions with a common denominator before combining numerators.

opening.prompt: Combine two fractional rates or parts.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make addition and subtraction necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for addition and subtraction.
exposition: Create equivalent rational expressions with a common denominator before combining numerators. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In addition and subtraction, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Shared-denominator construction. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Sign-distribution panel. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Clear denominators to produce candidates and verify every candidate in the original equation. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In rational equations, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

LCD applied to equation. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Candidate pipeline. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Rational Expressions, Equations, and Variation
unit.act: Act X - Tracking where division is allowed
unit.role: Develop algebra with variable denominators, explicit restrictions, and inverse variation.
unit.governingQuestion: What changes when a variable expression appears in a denominator?
unit.storyArc: A denominator creates excluded inputs. Factoring enables cancellation but cannot restore missing domain points. Common denominators permit addition and equation solving; sign analysis introduces rational inequalities and discontinuities.
outcomes: Identify excluded values and preserve original restrictions.
Simplify and perform arithmetic with rational expressions.
Solve rational equations and check candidate solutions.
Simplify complex rational expressions.
Model variation and interpret holes and asymptotes informally.
unit.investigation: Compare equivalent-looking rational formulas and explain how a missing input changes the graph or context.
unit.mastery: Every answer must include restrictions and rational-equation candidates must be checked in the original equation.

Radicals, Rational Exponents, and Complex Numbers
How do we reverse powers, and what happens when the real numbers are insufficient?

unit.title: Radicals, Rational Exponents, and Complex Numbers
unit.shortTitle: Radicals, Rational Exponents, and Complex Numbers
unit.act: Act XI - Reversing powers and enlarging the number system
unit.role: Develop exact root arithmetic, radical equations, extraneous-solution logic, and basic complex arithmetic.
unit.governingQuestion: How do we reverse powers, and what happens when the real numbers are insufficient?
unit.storyArc: General roots and rational exponents express inverse powers. Radical arithmetic creates exact forms, conjugates rationalize denominators, and raising powers solves equations but may introduce candidates. Complex numbers complete quadratic solutions.
outcomes: Interpret principal and general roots.
Simplify and combine radical expressions.
Rationalize denominators using factors or conjugates.
Connect radicals and rational exponents.
Solve radical equations and perform basic complex arithmetic.
unit.investigation: Compare reversible and nonreversible algebraic steps and explain exactly where extraneous candidates enter.
unit.mastery: Students preserve domains, simplify exact forms, check radical candidates, and express nonreal quadratic roots correctly.

unitLessons.title: General nth roots and principal roots
unitLessons.outcome: Distinguish the principal root operation from finding every solution of a power equation.

opening.prompt: Compare root notation with the solutions to x^2=9.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make general nth roots and principal roots necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for general nth roots and principal roots.
exposition: Distinguish the principal root operation from finding every solution of a power equation. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In general nth roots and principal roots, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Odd/even root graphs. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Principal-root selector. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

definitions.term: General nth roots and principal roots
definitions.definition: Distinguish the principal root operation from finding every solution of a power equation. The term names the lesson’s central relationship and the conditions under which its methods are valid.
definitions.conditions: Preserve the original domain, units, grouping, direction, and equivalence conditions whenever they apply.

definitions.definition: A justified change of form that preserves the value, truth set, relationship, or solution information required by the original problem.
definitions.conditions: One-way operations can create candidates and therefore require checking in the original statement.

examples.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 5 cups of flour. Find the water needed for 20 cups of flour.
steps: Write the ordered ratio 3/5 = w/20.
Multiply both sides by 20.
Check that 12/20 reduces to 3/5.
examples.answer: 12 cups of water
examples.interpretation: The scale factor from 5 to 20 is 4, so the water quantity also scales by 4.

examples.prompt: Represent the result of this general nth roots and principal roots case in a second form: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 5 cups of flour. Find the water needed for 20 cups of flour.
steps: Complete the calculation or classification before changing representations.
Choose a table, graph, number line, diagram, or equivalent symbolic form that preserves the same quantities.
Label the input, output, units, restrictions, or endpoints that carry mathematical meaning.
examples.answer: A correctly labeled second representation that preserves 12 cups of water.
examples.interpretation: The second form must communicate the same relationship, not merely repeat the symbols from the first form.

examples.prompt: A classmate reaches “12 cups of water” in a radicals, rational exponents, and complex numbers problem. Decide whether the reasoning is valid and justify the decision from the original conditions.
steps: Restate the original condition and identify any domain, unit, sign, or equivalence requirement.
Reproduce the decisive operation using the worked case.
Check the proposed result against the original statement and explain the conclusion.
examples.answer: The result is valid only when the reproduced work and original-condition check both support 12 cups of water.

opening.prompt: Decompose an area or length under a radical.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.

exposition: Extract perfect-power factors and retain exact form. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In simplifying radicals, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Factor tree under radical. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Square-area decomposition. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

opening.prompt: Solve a quadratic with negative discriminant.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.

exposition: Extend arithmetic consistently using i^2=-1 and represent nonreal roots. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In complex numbers and conjugates, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Complex plane. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Powers-of-i cycle. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Simplifying radicals
lesson.outcome: Extract perfect-power factors and retain exact form.

opening.prompt: Decompose an area or length under a radical.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make simplifying radicals necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for simplifying radicals.
exposition: Extract perfect-power factors and retain exact form. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In simplifying radicals, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Factor tree under radical. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Square-area decomposition. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: Factor x² − 5x + 6 completely and verify the result.
steps: Find two integers whose product is 6 and whose sum is −5.
Write the product (x − 2)(x − 3).

examples.interpretation: The factors expose the zeros 2 and 3 while expansion confirms equivalence.

opening.prompt: Rewrite an exact ratio into a conventional denominator form.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.

exposition: Multiply by a form of one to remove a radical denominator. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In rationalizing monomial denominators, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Equivalent-fraction multiplier. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Denominator transformation. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 5 cups of flour. Find the water needed for 20 cups of flour.

exposition: Extend arithmetic consistently using i^2=-1 and represent nonreal roots. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In complex numbers and conjugates, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Complex plane. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Powers-of-i cycle. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Functions as a Unifying Language
unit.act: Act XII - Organizing algebra around input and output
unit.role: Consolidate earlier relationships into function language without preempting full Precalculus theory.
unit.governingQuestion: How can one input-output framework organize the algebraic families already studied?
unit.storyArc: Relations become functions when each input has one output. Function notation separates evaluation from solving; domain and range collect restrictions and outputs; piecewise functions and arithmetic unify earlier examples.
outcomes: Determine whether a relation is a function.
Evaluate functions and solve output equations.
Determine domain and range from formulas, graphs, and contexts.
Interpret graph behavior and piecewise rules.
Combine functions arithmetically while tracking domain.
unit.investigation: Choose among linear, quadratic, rational, radical, and exponential models for unlabeled data or graphs.
unit.mastery: Students move among table, graph, formula, and context and distinguish evaluation from solving.

unitLessons.title: Relations and functions
unitLessons.outcome: Define a function as exactly one output for each allowed input.

opening.prompt: Classify tables, mappings, and graphs.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make relations and functions necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for relations and functions.
exposition: Define a function as exactly one output for each allowed input. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In relations and functions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Mapping diagrams. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Discrete and continuous relations. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Find every input that produces a requested output. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make range and graph behavior necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for range and graph behavior.
exposition: Read output sets, intervals of change, extrema, and intercepts from graphs and contexts. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In range and graph behavior, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Annotated graph. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Vertical/horizontal probes. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

opening.prompt: Match unlabeled tables, graphs, and formulas.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make comparing algebraic families necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for comparing algebraic families.
exposition: Identify change patterns, restrictions, and characteristic graph shapes across major families. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In comparing algebraic families, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Family gallery. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Linked representations. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Algebra
unit.act: Act XIII - Describing multiplicative change and undoing it
unit.role: Complete the Algebra course with repeated proportional change, inverse exponentiation, and equation solving.
unit.governingQuestion: How do we describe multiplicative change and solve for an unknown exponent?
unit.storyArc: Constant differences are contrasted with constant ratios. Repeated percentages produce exponential models, compounding motivates e, and logarithms reverse exponentiation. Log laws follow from exponent laws and solve previously inaccessible equations.
outcomes: Distinguish additive from multiplicative patterns.
Construct and interpret exponential growth and decay models.
Use compound and continuous growth formulas.
Define logarithms as inverse exponentiation and use log laws.
Solve exponential and logarithmic equations with domain checks.
unit.investigation: Compare linear, exponential, and logarithmic claims made from the same data and decide which conclusions are justified.
unit.mastery: Students construct models, solve exact and approximate equations, and reject logarithmic candidates outside the domain.

unitLessons.title: Additive versus multiplicative patterns
unitLessons.outcome: Distinguish constant difference from constant ratio in tables, graphs, and contexts.

opening.prompt: Compare equal-dollar growth with equal-percent growth.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make additive versus multiplicative patterns necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for additive versus multiplicative patterns.
exposition: Distinguish constant difference from constant ratio in tables, graphs, and contexts. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In additive versus multiplicative patterns, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. exposition: Motivate e through increasingly frequent compounding and use continuous growth/decay models. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In continuous growth and e, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

e^x graph. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

opening.prompt: Compare equal-dollar growth with equal-percent growth.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.

exposition: Distinguish constant difference from constant ratio in tables, graphs, and contexts. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In additive versus multiplicative patterns, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Arithmetic/geometric tables. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Linear/exponential graph comparison. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Interpret f(x)=ab^x, parameter restrictions, initial value, and growth or decay. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In exponential functions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Parameter-controlled graph. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Initial-value marker. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Compound interest
lesson.outcome: Compare compounding periods and calculate accumulated balance.

opening.prompt: Grow an account with periodic compounding.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make compound interest necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for compound interest.
exposition: Compare compounding periods and calculate accumulated balance. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In compound interest, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Account timeline. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Compounding partitions. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Interpret log_b(y) as the exponent producing y and state base/argument restrictions. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In logarithms as inverse operations, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make solving logarithmic equations and logarithmic models necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for solving logarithmic equations and logarithmic models.
exposition: Condense, exponentiate, and reject candidates with invalid log arguments. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In solving logarithmic equations and logarithmic models, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Domain-first number line. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Candidate check. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

Use compound and continuous growth formulas.
Define logarithms as inverse exponentiation and use log laws.
Solve exponential and logarithmic equations with domain checks.

unitLessons.title: Classifying mathematical objects
unitLessons.outcome: Identify whether a prompt contains an expression, equation, inequality, system, or function and determine the requested action.

opening.prompt: Sort a mixed collection of unlabeled tasks.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make classifying mathematical objects necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for classifying mathematical objects.
exposition: Identify whether a prompt contains an expression, equation, inequality, system, or function and determine the requested action. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In classifying mathematical objects, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Object sorting board. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Structure tree. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.title: Choosing a solving method
unitLessons.outcome: Select inverse operations, factoring, square roots, formulas, denominator clearing, powers, or logarithms based on structure.

opening.prompt: Plan the first move before doing arithmetic.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make choosing a solving method necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for choosing a solving method.
exposition: Select inverse operations, factoring, square roots, formulas, denominator clearing, powers, or logarithms based on structure. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In choosing a solving method, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Strategy tree. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Valid-method comparison. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 5 cups of flour. Find the water needed for 20 cups of flour.
steps: Write the ordered ratio 3/5 = w/20.
Multiply both sides by 20.
Check that 12/20 reduces to 3/5.
examples.answer: 12 cups of water
examples.interpretation: The scale factor from 5 to 20 is 4, so the water quantity also scales by 4.

examples.interpretation: The second form must communicate the same relationship, not merely repeat the symbols from the first form.

steps: Restate the original condition and identify any domain, unit, sign, or equivalence requirement.

Check the proposed result against the original statement and explain the conclusion.
examples.answer: The result is valid only when the reproduced work and original-condition check both support 12 cups of water.
examples.interpretation: A transferred method is complete only after its conditions and conclusion are checked in context.

lesson.title: Classifying mathematical objects
lesson.outcome: Identify whether a prompt contains an expression, equation, inequality, system, or function and determine the requested action.

opening.prompt: Sort a mixed collection of unlabeled tasks.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make classifying mathematical objects necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for classifying mathematical objects.
exposition: Identify whether a prompt contains an expression, equation, inequality, system, or function and determine the requested action. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In classifying mathematical objects, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Object sorting board. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Structure tree. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for choosing a solving method.
exposition: Select inverse operations, factoring, square roots, formulas, denominator clearing, powers, or logarithms based on structure. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In choosing a solving method, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Strategy tree. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Valid-method comparison. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Graphical and algebraic cross-checking
lesson.outcome: Use graphs for plausibility and solution count and algebra for exact justification.

opening.prompt: Compare equation intersections with symbolic roots.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make graphical and algebraic cross-checking necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for graphical and algebraic cross-checking.
exposition: Use graphs for plausibility and solution count and algebra for exact justification. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In graphical and algebraic cross-checking, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Intersection graph. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Sign/solution count. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.
